analysis.one_liner: Expands the Supreme Court from nine to thirteen justices.
analysis.headline: The bill to expand the Supreme Court from 9 to 13 justices never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Edward Markey's bill would have added four seats to the Supreme Court, growing it from 9 to 13 justices. Because new justices are appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate, adding four seats would have flipped the Court's current 6-3 conservative majority to a 7-6 majority — affecting how it rules on abortion, voting rights, guns, climate rules, and more. The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced in May 2023, and the committee never held a hearing or a vote on it. It died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the bill would have shifted the Supreme Court from a 6-3 conservative supermajority to a 7-6 balance, changing how the Court would rule on abortion access, voting rights, gun regulation, climate rules, and the power of federal agencies. People who support those outcomes — and the Democratic officeholders whose agenda has repeatedly lost 6-3 before the current Court — would have gained. The four new justices' seats would have been filled by the sitting Democratic president and Senate at the time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who want a less conservative Court

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the Court's size from 9 to 13 justices — one Chief Justice and 12 associates — by rewriting Title 28 of the U.S. Code, and raises the quorum needed to decide cases from 6 justices to 8.

Four additional seats would shift the Court's current 6-3 conservative majority to a 7-6 balance, giving cases on abortion, voting rights, guns, and federal regulatory power a different possible outcome — the stated purpose of the bill's supporters.
The bill is a single provision: it does not change the justices' lifetime tenure, nomination process, or jurisdiction, so its entire effect runs through the new seats and the quorum change.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have fallen on the current Court majority and the legal and political movement aligned with it, which would lose its hold on a solid 6-3 majority. The institution itself would also bear a cost: adding seats to flip a majority is widely criticized as court-packing, and it invites the other party to expand the Court the next time it holds power.

drawbacks.text: Adding exactly four justices — enough to flip the current 6-3 conservative majority to a 7-6 one — is hard to frame as a neutral structural reform; critics across the political spectrum call it court-packing, and it would invite the next party in power to expand the Court again, fueling a spiral that makes the Court's composition swing with every election and weakens its claim to independence.

The bill changes only the number of seats, not how justices are chosen or how long they serve; the new justices would be life-tenured appointees named by whoever holds the presidency and confirmed by whichever party holds the Senate, so the bill's effect depends entirely on winning two elections first.
The bill received no committee hearing, no markup, and no floor vote in two years, so there was never any public vetting of its design, its costs, or its legal consequences.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its own terms the bill is a straightforward lever: four more seats would flip a 6-3 conservative majority to a 7-6 one, potentially restoring access to abortion, broader voting protections, and a friendlier regulatory climate. The honest drawback is design, not just politics: adding exactly enough seats to flip a Court that is currently deciding for the governing party's opponents looks like a power move rather than a neutral reform, and once done, it is hard to un-do the next time the other party holds the White House and Senate. The strongest good-faith objection is that repeated expansions would shrink the Court into a prize that changes hands with each election, weakening its independence. Weighing that against the stakes the Court now decides — abortion, voting, guns, climate — supporters would argue the trade is worth it; skeptics would say the bill traded legitimacy for advantage. In any case, it never got far enough for anyone to test that trade: it sat without a hearing until the Congress ended.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the Judiciary Act of 2023 on May 16, 2023, a one-section bill amending Title 28 of the U.S. Code to allow 12 associate justices alongside the Chief Justice, up from the current 8 associates.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced. That referral was the last action ever taken on it.
The committee never held a hearing, never voted the bill out (called a markup), and the Senate never debated it on the floor, so the public never saw a roll-call vote on expanding the Court.
Only two Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors over the bill's entire life, reflecting how little support it gathered even within the majority party.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025; bills that do not pass before a Congress ends are dead and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The current 6-3 conservative Supreme Court majority keeps its power, and the senators and allied groups who preferred that no expansion ever be debated are better off. Ordinary people left the 118th Congress with the same Court they started with.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Court's current majority and its allies

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand the Court from 9 to 13 justices and sought cosponsors.

for.name: Two Democratic senators (cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Dick Durbin)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote. The committee's chair, a Democrat from the same party as the bill's sponsors, never scheduled it.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Uniformly opposed adding seats to the Court and would have blocked it on the floor even if the committee had advanced it.

against.name: President Joe Biden
against.what_they_did: Declined to endorse adding seats; his 2021 commission on the Court declined to recommend expansion, signaling the White House would not push the bill.

sides.party_line_note: There were no roll-call votes, but the bill's support was entirely Democratic — three Democratic senators — while Republicans opposed Court expansion across the board, and even Democratic committee leadership declined to move it.

industries.industry: The current Supreme Court majority and its governing coalition
industries.note: Adding four justices would end the 6-3 conservative majority's control over rulings on abortion, voting, guns, and federal regulation. This is a concentrated interest in institutional power rather than a commercial industry, and it is the group the bill is written against.

industries.industry: Business and industry litigants before the Court
industries.note: Court composition shapes how easily unions can organize, how strictly workplace, environmental, and consumer rules are enforced, and how much campaign money can flow in politics. The bill would change who wins those cases, though the direction for any given industry depends on its relationship to regulation.
